name: Thermochemistry
tagline: Heat flow, enthalpy, and energy changes in chemical reactions.
seo_title: Thermochemistry — paper summaries, news & innovations | Chemisters
seo_description: Follow Chemisters Thermochemistry on LinkedIn and Facebook: paper summaries, news and innovations in calorimetry, enthalpy, fuels and the energetics of reactions.

definition.lead: Thermochemistry measures the heat that flows in and out of chemical reactions and changes of state.
definition.body: Every fuel, every cold pack and every metabolic pathway is an energy balance. With enthalpies of formation and Hess's law, chemists can predict the heat of reactions they have never run.

released per mole of methane burned

branches.name: Calorimetry
branches.example: Bomb calorimeters give the energy values printed on food labels.

branches.name: Enthalpies of formation
branches.summary: The heat of making a compound from its elements.
branches.example: Tables of them give the ΔH of almost any reaction.

branches.name: Hess's law
branches.summary: The heat of a reaction does not depend on the route.
branches.example: Finding ΔH for C → CO from combustion data.

branches.name: Fuels & combustion
branches.summary: Comparing how much energy different fuels release.
branches.example: Energy per kilogram of hydrogen, petrol and coal.

branches.name: Phase changes
branches.summary: Latent heats of melting, boiling and sublimation.
branches.example: Sweating cools the body through evaporation.

branches.name: Bond enthalpies
branches.summary: Estimating reaction heats from the bonds broken and formed.
branches.example: Why burning hydrocarbons releases so much energy.

branches.name: Free energy & spontaneity
branches.summary: Combining heat and entropy to predict direction.

branches.name: Bioenergetics
branches.summary: How living cells capture and spend energy.

timeline.title: Latent heat
timeline.text: Joseph Black finds that melting ice absorbs heat without warming up.
timeline.why: Separated the ideas of heat and temperature.

timeline.title: The ice calorimeter
timeline.text: Antoine Lavoisier and Pierre-Simon Laplace measure heat by the amount of ice it melts.
timeline.why: Showed that respiration is a slow combustion.

timeline.title: Hess's law
timeline.text: Germain Hess shows that the total heat of a reaction is independent of the path.
timeline.why: Made it possible to compute heats that cannot be measured directly.

timeline.title: The mechanical equivalent of heat
timeline.text: James Joule measures how much work produces a given amount of heat.
timeline.why: Heat is a form of energy.

timeline.title: The laws of thermodynamics
timeline.text: Rudolf Clausius states the first and second laws in modern form.
timeline.why: The framework of all energy calculations.

timeline.title: Free energy
timeline.text: Josiah Willard Gibbs begins publishing his theory of chemical equilibrium.
timeline.why: Combined heat and entropy in one quantity.

timeline.title: Nernst's heat theorem
timeline.text: Walther Nernst formulates what becomes the third law.
timeline.why: Allowed equilibria to be computed from heat data.

timeline.title: Thermodynamics for chemists
timeline.text: G. N. Lewis and Merle Randall publish their textbook on free energy of chemical substances.
timeline.why: Organized thermochemical data for practical use.

timeline.title: Close to absolute zero
timeline.text: Nobel Prize to William Giauque for low-temperature chemical thermodynamics.

timeline.title: The ATP machine
timeline.text: Nobel Prize to Boyer and Walker for the mechanism of ATP synthase, shared with Jens Skou.
timeline.why: Explained how cells store chemical energy.

quiz.q: For an exothermic reaction, ΔH is…
quiz.explain: The system loses heat to the surroundings.

options: The total ΔH is the same whatever the route
Heat flows from cold to hot
quiz.explain: Enthalpy is a state function: only the start and end points matter.

quiz.q: The standard enthalpy of formation of O₂ gas is…
quiz.explain: By definition, elements in their standard state have ΔHf° = 0.

quiz.q: Why does an ammonium nitrate cold pack feel cold?
quiz.explain: The dissolution absorbs heat from its surroundings, including your hand.

quiz.q: A bomb calorimeter measures heat at constant…
quiz.explain: The sealed steel vessel keeps volume fixed, so it measures ΔU.

quiz.q: Why is a steam burn at 100 °C worse than a burn from water at 100 °C?
options: Steam releases its heat of vaporization as it condenses on the skin
Steam is always hotter than boiling water
Steam contains acid that attacks the skin
Steam is denser, so it presses heat into the skin
quiz.explain: Condensing water releases about 40 kJ per mole on top of the hot water itself.

quiz.q: In q = mcΔT, c stands for…
quiz.explain: The heat needed to warm 1 g of the substance by 1 °C.

quiz.q: Estimating ΔH from bond enthalpies: ΔH ≈ …
quiz.explain: Breaking bonds costs energy; forming bonds releases it.
Gibbs energy weighs heat against entropy.

quiz.q: Who stated the law of constant heat summation in 1840?
quiz.explain: Hess was a Swiss-born chemist working in Saint Petersburg.

quiz.q: Burning 1 mol of methane releases about 890 kJ. How much does burning 2 mol release?
quiz.explain: Enthalpy is extensive: double the amount, double the heat.

quiz.q: Water's unusually high heat capacity comes mainly from…
quiz.explain: Much of the added energy goes into stretching and breaking hydrogen bonds.
